svg.text: HashLife above a memo floor, the rule as a circuit of logic gates below it
Every picture and number is drawn from the measurement harness.
How a universe advances, and the words used below; the number on a step is the panel that shows it. The parts were measured separately: GHL has not yet run as one program.
The universe: a grid of tile IDs
The cells are cut into square tiles of side s. Equal tiles
get the same ID, so the GPU holds a grid of numbers,
Hit path: one probe per tile
A window (2×2 tiles) fixes its centre tile s/2
generations ahead. The memo is a table of windows
seen before; a probe looks one up.
Hit: the window is in the memo. Its future centre tile is
read off, no cell is touched, and the grid is s/2
The floor is the smallest window that is memoized.
Smaller ones cost more to look up than to compute.
Miss path: waves, one per level
Miss: not in the memo. The window is built from
windows half its size, which may miss too. A wave: all
misses of one size, as one batch.
At the floor: an atlas of windows
Missed floor windows are not split. They are laid side
by side, the atlas, and stepped cell by cell:
Brute force is a network of logic gates that updates 32
cells per operation. Its results go into the memo.
the results are stored in the memo, and the probes that missed now hit
How far each part is built
built and measured on the GPU
the CPU reference engine: not yet on the GPU
model: operation counts at measured rates
real patterns, named by their files; colour is the cell state

svg.text: Curves: how much of each universe is new, as the share of probes that miss, against the generations run so far (log scale); tiles of 16×16 cells, for Life 32×32. The number is that share over the second half of the run. The ROM's curve is

that of lotr1.PPMd-244K.rle, a smaller ROM of the same kind (1,548 × 1,461 cells); the soup's, that of a 512 × 512 soup. This novelty, not density, decides how a universe is best advanced: the ROM is new for one period and then
entirely known; the soup stays new.
Below the floor: the rule as a circuit
Hutton32b, 32 states, as a network of two-input gates
built and measured on the GPU
32 cells of squares.rle (marked in panel 3) and their four neighbours.
A state is 5 bits; bit k of 32 cells in a row is one 32-bit word: 25 words go in, 5 come out.
Checked while drawing: on all 357,120 cells of
this frame the network gives the next generation
of the pattern's own rule table, Hutton32.
entries. Mismatches on all of them: 0.

Every gate works on a 32-bit word, so it serves 32 cells at once. Wire shade: on how many of the 32 cells the signal is 1 (light: none, dark: all). A signal with several consumers is one wire with branches.
A two-state rule such as Life needs one bit per cell. An adder tree counts the live neighbours of 32 cells in 26 operations;
birth and survival are read off the four bits of the count.
Brute force as measured, in cell-updates per second
Above the floor: tiles, IDs and a memo table
the hit path: four IDs read, one probe
the hit path runs on the GPU
squares.rle at generation 20,480, cut into 16×16-cell tiles. One pass over the grid, a sweep, advances it 8 generations
with one probe per tile: 1,472 probes for 651 distinct windows, 103 misses (7.0 %, marked). The misses sit where the circuit
is computing; everything else is a hit. The white frame is taken apart on the right.
A tile's ID is its place in the
store of tiles, so equal tiles
universe is a grid of IDs: 4
A window is then four IDs: the
memo is looked up by IDs,
A memo entry: four IDs give one ID
the key: the four IDs framed above
A 32×32 window and the 16×16 tile in its centre 8 generations later. In this sweep the entry was not
there yet: a miss. Checked while drawing: the circuit of panel 2, applied 8 times, gives the same
The memo table, slot by slot
The first 3,840 of 1,048,576 slots (32 MiB) after 65,536 generations of squares.rle: a hash table
with linear probing, 1.49 probes per insert. 1.17·107 probes met 520,613 distinct windows. The
brute force under them amounts to 3.3 % of the cell-updates delivered; the rest came out of the
A miss: the recursion in waves, level by level
depth per universe and per region: model
One wave per level, each one batch for the GPU
A missed window is built from nine windows half its size and then four more: two waves, one
level down. Each box is a wave; its number is the windows that missed in it, its dark part their
share of the windows it asked for.
squares.rle, the 64 generations from 20,480: mostly known
lotr1.PPMd-244K.rle, a ROM, its first 64 generations: all new
35 and 36 waves end in brute force on 2,918 and 573,210 floor windows. A wave is 16 GPU
calls (dispatches) of fixed size: 50 µs measured for an empty one.
At the floor: an atlas of missed windows
35 of the 203 windows of one floor wave of squares.rle.
Each missed 16×16 window is copied from its four 8×8 tiles into one grid, the
atlas. The circuit of panel 2 steps the whole grid 4 generations, and the centre of
every window (outlined) becomes a tile with an ID. Every stage of a wave is one
GPU call over the whole batch. Above the floor a miss costs probes and inserts
Per universe: how deep the recursion may go
A GPU call costs at least 3.2 µs, however little it does, and every generation
needs several. Few active cells cannot pay for them: the smaller the universe, the
coarser its floor. The model's thresholds for Hutton32b:

svg.text: brute force, memo only above: 42 regions
256×256-cell regions, coloured by what they spent
most of the first 1,024 generations in. Where
content is new at every scale
part of the movie) every probe would miss, so the
region is stepped by brute force. The rest keeps its
memo. Model time for those generations: 18.6 ms;
Why a floor, and what it buys
A probe costs as much as ρ = RB / RP cell-updates of brute force: RB is the rate of brute
force, RP that of probes. RP is the same for every rule; RB is not. Per second:
What a hit saves, V / ρ. A w×w window gives its centre w/4 generations later: V = w3/16 cell-updates
1×: a hit saves what a probe costs
A window is worth a memo entry only if a hit saves more than the probe costs: from 16×16
windows on for Hutton32b (3.2×; 8×8 windows: 0.40×) and from 32×32 for Life (5.4×;
16×16: 0.67×). That is each rule's floor: a larger ρ puts it one level coarser. Golly's HashLife
memoizes down to 4×4 blocks, worth V = 4.
Against Golly 5.1, HashLife at its best step size: rate of the GHL part that ran, over Golly's

svg.text: on the GPU, measured and verified
the same, with the time to fill the memo on the CPU
the recursion on one CPU thread
Golly leads where content recurs sparsely and runs are long; there GHL falls back to the recursion on the CPU. Every GPU result was checked
against the CPU, and the CPU engine's final states equal Golly's.
